The Moon. Earth's only natural satellite, orbiting approximately 384,400 kilometers away and tidally locked so that one face always points toward Earth. Formed roughly 4.5 billion years ago from the debris of a giant impact, known as the Giant Impact Hypothesis, the Moon profoundly influences Earth's tides and axial stability. Its exploration during the Apollo program from 1969 to 1972 remains humanity's only crewed journey beyond Earth.

The lunar orbit period, called the sidereal month, is 27.3 days. The synodic month, which tracks lunar phases, is 29.5 days because Earth moves in its orbit during this time.

Tides are primarily caused by the Moon's gravity. The near side of Earth is pulled harder than the center, creating a tidal bulge on the near side and on the far side simultaneously.

The Moon is tidally locked. The same face always points toward Earth because its rotation period matches its orbital period, a consequence of Earth's tidal braking over billions of years.

Lunar surface features include craters, impact sites from asteroids and meteorites; maria, dark lowland plains from ancient volcanic eruptions; and highlands, ancient raised terrain.

Apollo 11 in 1969 achieved the first crewed lunar landing when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. Six crewed landings occurred between 1969 and 1972, bringing back 380 kilograms of lunar samples.

The Moon lacks a significant atmosphere because its escape velocity is too low and solar wind strips gases away. The lunar surface experiences extreme temperatures of 120 degrees Celsius in sunlight and minus 170 degrees Celsius in darkness, with no weather.

Lunar mass is approximately one-eighty-first of Earth's mass. Gravity at the lunar surface is about one-sixth of Earth's, allowing astronauts to jump far higher.

The Giant Impact Hypothesis proposes that a Mars-sized body collided with the early Earth approximately 4.5 billion years ago, with debris from the impact coalescing into the Moon.
